title: A leaf that learned to drift

events.text: A leaf that learned to drift. I am painting an imagined leafy sea dragon in blue-green water, inspired by the Aquarium of the Pacific species guide. Goal: a continuous curved body, filled leaf lobes, and open water between them. Begin with long water washes.
The first four washes left wide pale seams. Bridge those before the animal; a continuous water field will make the leaf gaps readable.
The water is continuous now, with quiet horizontal bands. Lay a curved ochre trunk and taper the tail toward the lower right; the head will turn left.
The trunk is filled and the tail tapers, but the head is only a hook. Join a small oval head and long leftward tube snout, then establish two leaf stems.
The head loop left a blue hollow. Fill through it now, then turn the first two stems into broad lobes with tapered ends.
The head hollow is closed. The first leaves read as solid paddles; give them unequal branching neighbors while preserving the blue wedge beside the neck.
The upper branches retain clear blue windows. The lower right stem is bare; add two unequal leaves and a smaller head frill.
The animal spans the water comfortably, but the leaves remain paired paddles. Add side lobes with unequal lengths; keep their joins filled rather than outlining loops.
The new lobes break the pairs but retain angular corners. Develop the trunk with sampled warm upper planes and cool undersides; let one continuous gesture carry the curve.
The upper plane bends smoothly; the underside is too dark and stripe-like. Soften it with a broader olive neighbor, and give the leaf surfaces gentle two-tone turns.
The broad olive neighbor reduced the harsh stripe, leaving a textured seam. The head still has no focus. Place a small dark eye and model the snout without enlarging it.

The small eye anchors the head and the snout reads as a tube. The requested upper focus reset during painting; this review is the centered close view. Add muted rose rib bands, following the trunk turn with unequal spacing.
Four muted ribs are visible without overwhelming the ochre body. Continue them smaller toward the tail, and add a narrow cheek shadow to separate head from neck.
The tapering ribs support the curve. The leaves still share a flat value; build darker folds on their lower sides while retaining light tips.
The shadow folds separate the leaves from their stems. Add smaller near-body frills to break the long bare neck and underside; leave the main blue windows open.
The two small frills break the bare body without closing the larger gaps. Their three-point tips look angular. Try sampled curved lobes at the head and tail before adding finer veins.

The sampled small lobes turn more gently than the earliest paddles, though their tips remain ridged. The water has no depth cue. Add subdued distant seagrass at the edges, keeping it away from the snout and body.
The distant grasses are extremely faint at whole view. Keep that quiet layer, but add four narrower oil blades at the margins so their curves survive stepping back.
The narrow oil grasses survive at the margins and stay below the snout. Return to the leaves: use thin curved center folds and short side notches, avoiding uniform outlines.
The center folds are subtle at whole view. The leaves are still broad paddles. Cut only four small water notches to break their edges, then inspect whether the new blue marks feel integrated.
The blue cuts landed inside the leaves and read as raised scratches rather than open notches. Repair their color with loaded green neighbors; do not repeat the cut elsewhere.

The green repairs reduced the blue scratches, leaving raised patches. Stop cutting those edges. Small translucent fins can distinguish the swimming body from its leaf frills; test two soft planes and their short roots.

The fin washes are barely visible; their short roots remain. The lower leaf repair still shows a blue remnant and the ribs are too uniform in strength. Use broad leaf planes and small ochre breaks to quiet those faults.

The broad leaf planes covered the blue remnants more completely. A lone pale fin root still looks like a whisker; join a small muted fin plane to it, and refine the head with short cheek and crest lights.
The fin root is now joined to a muted plane; head lights remain restrained. Test one tiny eye reflection alone. It should keep the head focal without becoming a large white spot.

The tiny reflection stays within the eye and survives whole view. Final refinement: quiet the fin brightness, connect a lower frill root, and soften one dark rib end. Then judge the complete light structure again.

Final review at 100 completed marks: a continuous curved trunk, filled unequal frills, open blue windows and a compact eye light hold together. The broad repairs reduced blue cuts but left raised patches; faceted leaves and regular bristles remain. Further covers would mainly add relief, so I will keep these irregularities and stop.

inspiration.title: Aquarium of the Pacific — Leafy Seadragon
inspiration.interpretation: Original imagined leafy sea dragon suspended diagonally above sparse seagrass in blue-green water; no finished composition copied. Journal searched for sea dragon/seadragon before choosing.
